extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary biography, religious history, and students of preaching/theology
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length biographical and critical account of John Bunyan's spiritual struggles, theology, and ministry, with embedded practical judgments about prayer, preaching, and religious pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prayer must be an expression of inward feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: "To be worth anything prayer must be the expression of an inward feeling; and that people cannot feel in lines laid down for them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms or set liturgies are criticized because they encourage rote words without inner feeling. The author reports Bunyan's explicit dislike of Liturgy on this ground and uses this standard to judge forms of worship as spiritually ineffective or even harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teaching children rote prayers; teach by conviction of sin
rubrics_metrics.description: "My judgment is that men go the wrong way to learn their children to pray. ... It seems to me a better way for people to tell their children betimes what cursed creatures they are... The way that men learn to pray is by conviction of sin, and this is the way to make our 'sweet babes' do so too."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogical recommendation: instead of teaching children fixed prayers, inculcate an awareness of sin, God's wrath, and the need for repentance so that prayer arises from genuine conviction. The author also cautions this method risks making children 'unreal' or exposing them to doctrines beyond their comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preaching should begin with sinners and be grounded in personal conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Lord led him to begin where his Word began--with sinners. ... I preached what I felt. I had been sent to my hearers as from the dead. I went myself in chains to preach to them in chains, and carried that fire in my own conscience that I persuaded them to beware of."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sermons ought to start from the concrete spiritual condition of listeners (their sin under the law vs. grace), use the 'terrors of the law' where appropriate, and be delivered with the preacher's authentic personal experience and conviction rather than abstract moralizing. Authenticity, personal struggle, and emotional engagement are presented as essential for effective preaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be adaptable in delivery and publish revised sermons
rubrics_metrics.description: "Bunyan preached wherever opportunity served--in woods, in barns, on village greens, or in town chapels. The substance of his sermons he revised and published."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance on ministry: use any available venue to preach, be willing to preach in informal settings, revise sermons for clarity or publication, and disseminate revised sermons to broader audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid introducing metaphysical conceptions of 'law' into religion
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is dangerous to introduce into religion metaphysical conceptions of 'law.' The cord cracks that is strained too tightly; and it is only for brief periods of high spiritual tension that a theology so merciless can sustain itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical standard for theology: while metaphysical analogies (law as an unchangeable axiom) can clarify certain doctrines, overusing them leads to an austere, brittle religion that cannot be sustained by most believers. The author warns against making theological systems that cannot be emotionally or morally borne by ordinary persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize human inability and substitutionary atonement (doctrinal content)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The law... allowed no repentance to those who lived and died under it. ... The substitution of Christ's perfect fulfilment of the law alone rescues us."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrinal criterion for preaching/teaching: present the seriousness of the law (human inability to fulfill it) and the necessity of Christ's substitutionary satisfaction. The text treats this as the theological core that produces gratitude and consequent devotion in the believer; it is both descriptive of Bunyan's message and a standard by which his preaching is judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor enthusiasm and heartfelt religion over cold appeals to duty
rubrics_metrics.description: "The enthusiasm which will stir men's hearts and give them a real power of resisting temptation must be nourished on more invigorating food. Appeals to a sense of duty do not reach beyond the understanding."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persuasive strategy guidance: to move people morally and spiritually, cultivate passionate, affecting religious content (stories, intense conviction) rather than relying chiefly on rational appeals to duty or dry moral exhortation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation for ministry: private testing of gifts with humility
rubrics_metrics.description: "After earnest entreaty, however, 'he made experiment of his powers' in private, and it was at once evident that, with the thing which these people meant by inspiration, he was abundantly supplied. ... In fear and trembling, therefore, he set himself to the work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline for those called to preach: test and practise one's gifts privately before public ministry; maintain humility and reverent fear about exercising a ministerial calling even when gifts are evident.
